records.title: Burak Çetin
records.text: 🗺️ 𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝗽𝘀, 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗼𝘁𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝘁: 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗥𝗢𝗦 𝟮? One of the classic headaches in robot mapping is that 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝘃𝗶𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 gets, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗥𝗔𝗠 your map eats. 𝗥𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴-𝗕𝗼𝗻𝘅𝗮𝗶 tackles exactly that problem. Developed by Mukund Bala in 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗿𝗻 𝗖++𝟭𝟳, this 𝗥𝗢𝗦 𝟮 𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗮𝗴𝗲 builds on the Bonxai voxel library and keeps only a local map around the robot in memory. As the robot moves, the map "𝗿𝗼𝗹𝗹𝘀" with it: regions that fall out of range are saved to disk in 𝗰𝗵𝘂𝗻𝗸𝘀, then loaded back automatically when the robot returns to them. 𝗔 𝗳𝗲𝘄 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝘁'𝘀 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗮 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸: 🪶 Lightweight and scalable, a good fit for drones and resource-limited embedded hardware 📦 Smart chunk-based loading and unloading that keeps memory usage under control 🤖 Built natively for 𝗥𝗢𝗦 𝟮 🌱 Open-source, with development still ongoing If your robots need to cover large areas without running out of memory, this approach is definitely worth exploring. 🔗𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆: https://lnkd.in/dJpz4TH7 #ROS2 #Robotics #SLAM #Mapping

records.text: Can a vertiport actually make money? I started from the bottom up — not with projected passenger demand, but with the smallest functional facility I could model: 1 TLOF, 2 stands, charging, ARFF and a 1,000 sqm terminal. The result surprised me. At full capacity, the facility generates about ₹3.4 crore in annual revenue, yet the project IRR is only around 2% — before land and taxes. The problem is not simply CAPEX. It is how much revenue a vertiport can extract from each four-seat aircraft movement without damaging the operator's economics. This is Part 1. The next question is whether a network of vertiports changes the economics. #Vertiports #AdvancedAirMobility #AirportPlanning #Aviation #InfrastructureFinance https://lnkd.in/dh8sNJnF

records.text: Burak Çetin поделился(ась) публикацией участника Kiwi Hsieh : Can AI learn to land a VTOL aircraft the way a human pilot does? ✈️ Recently, I've been developing an AI Pilot prototype using Imitation Learning / Behavior Cloning to learn VTOL flight-control behavior from human pilot demonstrations. The current model is a GRU-based Behavior Cloning model, trained using aircraft flight states and human pilot demonstrations. In this simulation, the AI Pilot takes over in QHOVER and successfully completes the landing. Because of the camera perspective, it may not be obvious in the video, but the AI actually takes over from around 15 m altitude and 30 m away from the landing point, then controls the aircraft through the full approach and landing. The complete pipeline is now connected: Human Flight Data → Model Training → Real-time AI Inference → ArduPilot Integration → Aircraft Response This is still an early-stage proof of concept, but the long-term goal is to explore more challenging VTOL operations such as ship landing, moving-platform landing, and non-GPS environments. records.text: Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope; NN verification tools exist, but they scale poorly and only cover narrow, pre-specified properties over bounded inputs, not the real world your vehicle actually flies through. The pattern (often called Simplex, after Lui Sha's original work at Illinois) is simple to state and hard to build correctly: run your high-performance ML controller as the primary. Run a much simpler, formally verifiable baseline controller in parallel — one that can't do the mission well, but can be proven never to violate the safety envelope. A decision module — the actual hard engineering problem — watches system state and switches to the baseline before the envelope is breached, not after. Get the switching logic wrong and you get two failure modes, both bad: switch too conservatively and your ML controller never gets to do anything interesting; switch too late and the baseline can't recover in time. The switching threshold has to be derived from your vehicle's actual dynamics and worst-case latency, not picked as a round number. This is also why RTA architecture keeps showing up in DoW flight test programs pairing aggressive ML controllers with certified safety systems and automatic recovery — the government isn't asking "is your AI good," it's asking "what happens in the 0.1% case, and can you prove it." If your pitch deck shows an ML controller with no separately-verified safety layer next to it, that's the first thing a government test team asks about — long before they ask about your accuracy numbers. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy

Sachin Jain, Ph.D. разместил(а) контент: You can't verify a neural network the way you can verify a PID controller — decades of control theory give you closed-form stability guarantees over the whole operating envelope; NN verification tools exist, but they scale poorly and only cover narrow, pre-specified properties over bounded inputs, not the real world your vehicle actually flies through. The pattern (often called Simplex, after Lui Sha's original work at Illinois) is simple to state and hard to build correctly: run your high-performance ML controller as the primary. Run a much simpler, formally verifiable baseline controller in parallel — one that can't do the mission well, but can be proven never to violate the safety envelope. A decision module — the actual hard engineering problem — watches system state and switches to the baseline before the envelope is breached, not after. Get the switching logic wrong and you get two failure modes, both bad: switch too conservatively and your ML controller never gets to do anything interesting; switch too late and the baseline can't recover in time. The switching threshold has to be derived from your vehicle's actual dynamics and worst-case latency, not picked as a round number. This is also why RTA architecture keeps showing up in DoW flight test programs pairing aggressive ML controllers with certified safety systems and automatic recovery — the government isn't asking "is your AI good," it's asking "what happens in the 0.1% case, and can you prove it." If your pitch deck shows an ML controller with no separately-verified safety layer next to it, that's the first thing a government test team asks about — long before they ask about your accuracy numbers. #DoW #Defense #Autonomy
